# Summary of Alfred North Whitehead
Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) was an English mathematician and philosopher notable for his collaborative work on *Principia Mathematica* with Bertrand Russell, a foundational text in mathematical logic. Initially focused on mathematics and physics, Whitehead shifted toward philosophy, developing a highly original metaphysical system known as process philosophy or the "philosophy of organism." He rejected the classical notion of reality as composed of separate, static material entities, instead conceiving reality as composed of interrelated events and processes of "becoming." Whitehead emphasized that all entities have experience and creativity to some degree and that relations are fundamental to existence, challenging Cartesian dualism and materialism.
Whitehead’s philosophical contributions include foundational works such as *A Treatise on Universal Algebra* (1898), *An Introduction to Mathematics* (1911), and *Process and Reality* (1929). His metaphysics, though dense and often regarded as difficult, remains influential in areas such as process theology, ecological ethics, education theory, and philosophical approaches to science. At Harvard, where he taught philosophy from 1924 until his retirement in 1937, Whitehead produced several key philosophical texts, including *Science and the Modern World* (1925). Whitehead also advocated for educational reform, emphasizing the importance of teaching interconnected, living ideas over inert facts and valuing imagination in learning. Despite limited mainstream recognition within dominant philosophical schools, his work has inspired theologians, scientists, ecologists, and educators worldwide.
